name: Schengen short-stay visa (Category C) / visa-free stay

requirements.blocker_text: Category C visas and visa-free entry cover tourism, business visits, and family visits; they do not authorise employment or self-employment in Poland.
requirements.fix_path: Apply for the relevant work or business residence route instead if the purpose is employment.

requirements.blocker_text: Applicants must show sufficient funds for the intended stay, commonly assessed around PLN 300/day of stay (or documented sponsorship/invitation covering costs), plus return travel and travel medical insurance of at least EUR 30,000.
requirements.fix_path: Provide bank statements, a sponsorship declaration, or a formal invitation covering the cost of stay.

requirements.blocker_text: Applicants must not be flagged in the Schengen Information System and must not be considered a threat to public policy, security, or health.

evidence_required.document: Valid travel document, valid at least 3 months beyond intended departure
Travel medical insurance, minimum EUR 30,000 coverage, valid for the Schengen area
Proof of purpose of visit, accommodation, and sufficient funds

outcome.duration_length: up to 90 days in any 180-day period
outcome.physical_presence_requirement: max 90 days per 180-day rolling window across the whole Schengen area, not just Poland

sources.title: gov.pl -- Uzyskaj wizę jednolitą Schengen (official Polish government visa portal)
Migrant.info.pl (IOM / Polish Ministry of Interior co-funded portal) -- Visas, corroborating the funds and insurance conditions
Deel -- How to Get a Visa and Work Permit in Poland (2025), corroborating the confirmed absence of a Polish digital-nomad visa

notes: Poland is a full Schengen member, so short-stay entry follows the standard EU Schengen Borders Code / common visa framework, not a Poland-specific instrument -- citizens of many countries (US, UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, etc.) enter visa-free under the same 90/180 rule and the same purpose and funds restrictions as Category C visa holders. Poland has no working-holiday agreement network on the scale of e.g. the Netherlands or Australia and no digital-nomad visa (confirmed absence noted repeatedly across immigration-law secondary sources, e.g. Deel's 2026 guide, and not contradicted by any tier-1 Polish source found), so remote workers who are not employed by a Polish entity have no dedicated short-stay-plus route beyond this one and must otherwise use the business-activity or single-permit routes if they intend a longer or working stay.
